newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Ex-Soviet states nervous at Afghan Taleban advance.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet states nervous at Afghan Taleban advance.

text.p: The former Soviet republics of Central Asia, alarmed by the rise of Moslem fundamentalism, hastily beefed up their border security on Sunday after advances by the radical Islamist Taleban militia in neighbouring Afghanistan.

Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are worried that the Taleban's capture on Saturday of the main northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif, a former stronghold of opposition chief General Abdual Rashid Dostum, could upset regional stability.
"Uzbekistan's border troops are taking measures to reinforce the (Afghan) border to exclude any provocations," said a statement issued by the foreign ministry in Tashkent.

"Talks with the border service on the Afghan side are underway to preserve calm and provide security for the population on both sides of the border," it said, adding that no border incidents had occurred so far.
On Sunday the Turkish foreign ministry announced that Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, had arrived in Ankara after fleeing Afghanistan. Earlier reports had said Dostum had gone to Uzbekistan.

A representative of the Russian border guards in Tajikistan told Reuters there had been an increased influx of refugees from Afghanistan into Tajikistan through the checkpoint at Nizhny Pyandzh, some 200 km (125 miles) south of the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov held talks with his security advisers late on Saturday on the Afghan crisis. Security officials also met on Sunday morning to discuss ways of maintaining stability.

Less than two weeks ago the Taleban government protested at being left out of a summit meeting of the 10-nation Economic Cooperation Organisation at Dushanbe, capital of Tajikistan, which was attended by ousted president Rabbani.
Russian border troops have also been put on alert in Kyrgyzstan, Interfax news agency said on Sunday.
In Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov warned the Taleban not to violate the borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), successor to the Sovet Union.

"(Any infringement) will provoke very tough and effective actions from the CIS side," Interfax news agency quoted Primakov as saying. On Saturday Moscow issued a statement expressing its alarm over events in Afghanistan.
Primakov has made clear that Moscow regards the Taleban as incapable of uniting Afghanistan because it lacks broad support among the country's many ethnic minorities, who include Tajiks and Uzbeks.
He said Pakistan and the intelligence services of several Western countries could help put pressure on the Taleban to behave with restraint.

Russia -- separated from Afghanistan by more than 1,000 km of Kazakhstan territory -- has some 20,000 troops stationed in Tajikistan, who guard the remote, mountainous Afghan border and view themselves as a shield against Islamist fundamentalism.
Last month Rakhmonov said that up to a million refugees could pour from Afghanistan into his impoverished country of 5.7 million people if there was fierce fighting in Afghanistan.
On Sunday Interfax quoted Tajik Foreign Minister Talbak Nazarov in the Iranian capital Tehran as saying that his war-ravaged country could not cope with such an influx.

"However our republic will not throw these people to the whim of fate and will make a contribution to helping them, though their best hope lies with other countries and with international organisations," Interfax quoted Nazarov as saying.
Rakhmonov's secular government and the united Islamist opposition agreed last year on a ceasefire to end a four-year civil war that left tens of thousands killed and drove many more from their homes.
